title: School Improvement, Informally
author: Nick Hart
summary: This article examines the largely undervalued role of informal leadership practices in school improvement, arguing that formality and informality are not opposites but complements — and that the most significant professional learning in schools happens through informal channels that leaders rarely design for deliberately. Nick Hart explores two domains where informality has particular leverage: professional development (CPD) and accountability systems. On CPD, he draws on research suggesting informal learning accounts for upward of 75% of total teacher learning, distinguishing individual from collaborative informal learning and intentional from incidental informal learning. On accountability, the piece argues that informal accountability — the relational pressure of professional norms, mutual observation, and collegial expectation — is both more prevalent and more effective than formal evaluation systems in shaping daily practice. The article calls on school leaders to recognize and intentionally cultivate informal leadership structures rather than treating them as what happens between the real work.
points: Informal learning accounts for upward of 75% of total teacher learning, dwarfing the structured CPD programmes that school leaders tend to design and invest in — yet informal learning rarely receives deliberate design attention.

Informality is not the opposite of formality in school leadership but its powerful complement: even highly formal systems like safeguarding depend on informal leadership behaviours — dropping in on vulnerable children, building parent relationships, correcting collegial misunderstandings in the moment.

Informal accountability — the relational pressure of professional norms, peer visibility, and collegial expectation — shapes daily classroom practice more powerfully and continuously than annual formal evaluation cycles.

School leaders who recognize that the most significant professional development happens in hallway conversations, collaborative planning, and impromptu classroom observations can begin to design for those conditions rather than treating them as fortunate accidents.

The distinction between intentional and incidental informal learning matters: leaders who surface and direct informal learning toward strategic priorities can leverage the 75% rather than leaving it to chance.
quotes: The level of formality in the leadership of schools is an interesting continuum. On the one hand, leaders need to establish systems, structures and rules of thumb to ensure the smooth running of the school. On the other hand, schools are so complex that such systems only go so far in mitigating that complexity.

Think of informality as a complement to formality (a powerful complement at that). Let's consider safeguarding. The formal leadership of safeguarding would involve systems for reporting, recording and acting on concerns or disclosures... Informal leadership of safeguarding would be more reactive and reflective when issues arise.

Informal learning has been found to be more prevalent with some estimates upwards of 75% of total learning engaged in by teachers. One way of conceiving of informal learning is whether it is individual or collaborative.

When leaders run structured training over a period of time on their strategic priorities, or send colleagues out to learn on courses such as NPQs, this is formal learning and it is this type of learning that we might bring to mind when thinking about developing our teachers.
There are two other domains of school leadership where informality has the potential to greatly enhance any formal systems that leaders might have and they are CPD and accountability systems.
For any action that leaders take, there are all sorts of consequences that might arise; some predictable and positive, some unpredictable and negative plus so much more.
